claims.text: Limited precursor mobility governs formation of single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticles through stochastic principles.
Rapid heating and cooling create the limited precursor mobility responsible for stochastic nucleation.
Stochastic nucleation favors random, homogeneous incorporation of five or more elements into a single-phase solid solution.
Greater precursor mobility enables atomic rearrangement and causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Greater precursor mobility causes altered particle morphology.
Greater precursor mobility causes premature high-temperature decomposition.
The initial material consists of five or more noble-metal single-source precursors intended to form single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Heating rate, cooling rate, or dwell time can be varied at fixed composition to modulate precursor mobility.
The relevant comparison is rapid heating and cooling against slower heating or a prolonged high-temperature dwell.
Limited mobility produces a kinetically trapped random alloy, whereas enhanced mobility facilitates elemental segregation and phase splitting.
Reduced diffusion time suppresses cooperative reduction and atomic rearrangement.
Under mobility-limited processing, nucleation occurs stochastically with locally random elemental incorporation.
When mobility increases, elemental atoms preferentially coalesce and produce phase separation and morphological irregularities.
Rapid baseline processing will yield homogeneous nanoparticles with single-phase diffraction and uniform elemental distributions.
Longer dwell times or slower cooling will produce phase separation, compositional segregation, and altered particle morphology.
Longer dwell times or slower cooling will shift characteristic thermal decomposition temperatures.
The mechanism applies generally to noble-metal nanoparticle systems containing more than five elements whenever available diffusion time is critical.
At sufficiently high mobility, thermodynamic-equilibrium segregation supersedes the mobility-limited mechanism.
The mobility thresholds separating stochastic trapping from rearrangement-driven segregation are unquantified and depend on precursor chemistry and elemental interactions.
A lack of systematic changes in phase purity, elemental distribution, and morphology upon changing heating and cooling rates would falsify mobility-controlled single-phase formation.
